summary: A humorous April 1 memo composed of letters that imagine a possible future viewed from the 21st century. It is informational and not a technical specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A set of pretend letters written from the future, just for fun and imagination.

questions: april first rfc letters from the future
subtitle: Letters from the year 2023, imagining how the Internet evolved

tldr.problem: It is April 1st, 1994. What will the Internet look like in 30 years?
tldr.mechanism: This RFC is framed as a series of email letters discovered in a time capsule, supposedly written in 2023 by researchers on Mars and the Moon. They discuss the history of the Internet, its growth from ARPANET through the 1990s and beyond, and speculate on future developments in computing, networking, and nanotechnology.
tldr.outcome: This is an April 1st RFC—it is pure speculative fiction for entertainment. But many of the concerns raised (exponential growth, address space exhaustion, multimedia protocols, security and cryptography) turned out to be real issues.

today: This is an April 1st RFC and is entirely fictional. The future it imagines is speculation written in 1994. However, many real concerns surfaced in the letters: address space exhaustion (which did lead to IPv6), multimedia standards challenges, cryptography policy debates, and the eventual ubiquity of networked computing. The memo is a humorous exploration of what technologists in 1994 imagined the future might hold.

sections.title: The April 1st Frame
sections.content:
This RFC, published on April 1st, 1994, is framed as a collection of email letters discovered in September 1993 in a reverse time capsule supposedly sent from 2023. The author, Vinton Cerf, notes that spectral analysis suggests the letters origin after 2020, but he cannot vouch for their accuracy. The letters are presented in full as the body of the memo, followed by a brief concluding section.

The conceit allows the RFC to discuss the history and evolution of the Internet from the perspective of researchers 30 years in the future, based on their exploration of historical archives.
sections.plainLanguage: Pretend emails from the future arrived in a time capsule. Scientists on Mars and the Moon talk about how the Internet grew.

sections.title: A Brief Internet History (From 2023's Perspective)
sections.content:
The letters document the Internet's origins in the 1960s: ARPANET work by ARPA, packet networks built by IRIA (now INRIA) in France, and early work in England on what became the first local area network. ALOHANET used shared radio channels, and Ethernet brought those ideas to coaxial cable at XEROX PARC.

By 1983, TCP/IP was mandatory across ARPANET and connected networks, marking the start of global Internet growth. By mid-1993 (from the 2023 viewpoint), over 15,000 networks and 2 million computers were connected. The NSF created five supercomputer centers and funded "intermediate level" networks that became commercial services. The system was doubling annually, attracting intense attention.

The letters discuss the IETF's struggle in 1991-1994 with the IP address space exhaustion problem and the effort to design a successor to IPv4. They also reference RFCs as the principal means of documenting Internet technology and culture, preserved in the Postel Historical Institute.
sections.plainLanguage: From 1960s military computers to thousands of connected networks by the 1990s. The researchers found old RFCs and emails from 50+ years before, in archives.

sections.title: Deployment and Growth (1980s-2000s Imagined)
sections.content:
The letters describe massive growth in routing equipment, workstations, servers, and networking. The last half of the 1980s saw rapid equipment market growth. By the late 1990s and beyond, the wide-area system migrated to ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) switching. End-to-end transfer rates reached gigabytes per second.

Gigabit-per-second networks emerged. All-optical transmission, switching, and computing eventually became cost-effective. By the 2000s-2020s, molecular fabrication techniques allowed nano-scale IPv9 protocol machines to be built. New access methods proliferated: mobile radio, satellite, dial-up ISDN, cable, and fiber-based services. Even bulletin board systems got connected to the Internet, creating new publishing environments where authors published directly.

Multimedia became standard, not a buzzword. Copyright issues were addressed through case law and digital rights management. Cryptography became essential for authentication and privacy, though governments initially resisted.
sections.plainLanguage: Networks got faster, cheaper, and more widespread. Everyone could send multimedia messages. Security and privacy became really important.

sections.title: Looking Forward from 2023
sections.content: From 2023's imagined vantage point, the researchers note that by 2003, address space issues had been solved (through IPv6 or similar means), mobile and dynamic addressing became central to the Internet, and the scale grew to billions of computers. One researcher jokes that the engineers of the 1990s "blew it when they picked a measly 64 bit address space"—they should have allocated 1024 bits to ensure enough room for "obvious applications." The letters close with speculation that many technical and policy questions remain to guide progress toward the dense information society they now inhabit.
sections.plainLanguage: By 2023, there are billions of computers connected. But even that is not enough space. The future is hard to predict.
